people.name: Luther Youngdahl
people.field: Public service, mental health and human services reform
body: On Halloween night in 1949, Governor Luther Youngdahl stood outside Anoka State Hospital before more than a thousand spectators and set fire to hundreds of straitjackets and other restraints that had been used on patients. MNopedia counts 671 straitjackets. The bonfire was political theater, and it was meant to be. Youngdahl wanted the public to see that the state was changing how it treated people in its institutions.

In the 1940s Minnesota ran a network of large state hospitals for people with mental illness and developmental disabilities. They were overcrowded, understaffed and largely hidden from public view. Change began from the ground up. Historian Susan Bartlett Foote's book The Crusade for Forgotten Souls, which won the 2019 Minnesota Book Award for Minnesota Nonfiction, credits a little-known hospital attendant, Engla Schey, the daughter of Norwegian immigrants, whose journals and outrage helped move reform-minded Unitarians to take up the cause. A 1948 report from a Unitarian committee, backed by Minneapolis Tribune coverage, put the problem in front of the public.

Youngdahl, a Republican first elected governor in 1946, took up the issue, even when it meant challenging members of his own party. He appointed a task force, and its recommendations moved the state's approach toward treatment and recovery rather than custody alone. He left the governorship in 1951, when President Truman appointed him a federal judge in Washington, D.C.

The legacy is complicated. The Anoka bonfire did not end the use of restraints in Minnesota. Restraint and seclusion in state programs later became the subject of the Jensen settlement against the Department of Human Services. A public turning point was the start of reform, not its end.
keyFacts: 1948: Unitarian committee report on state hospital conditions.
October 31, 1949: Burned restraints at Anoka State Hospital.
1951: Appointed to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

people.name: Elizabeth Kenny
body: In 1940 an Australian bush nurse arrived in the United States with a treatment for polio that most American doctors had never seen. The standard approach then was to immobilize paralyzed limbs in splints and casts. Elizabeth Kenny, known by her Australian nursing title "Sister Kenny," did the opposite. She used hot, moist packs to relieve muscle spasms and then gently retrained muscles through movement.

Doctors in New York and Chicago dismissed her ideas, but in Minnesota she found an interested audience. She demonstrated her treatments with the Mayo Clinic and the University of Minnesota, and in 1942 became a guest instructor at the University of Minnesota Medical School.

The city backed her. The Minneapolis Board of Public Welfare suggested its Lymanhurst building, then a school and hospital for children with rheumatic fever, and remodeled it for her work. The Elizabeth Kenny Clinic opened there on December 17, 1942, and became the Sister Kenny Institute in 1943. It trained nurses and physical therapists in what became known as the Kenny Method. MNopedia says children and young adults traveled from around the world to be treated by her.

Kenny returned to Australia and died in Toowoomba, Queensland, in 1952. After the polio vaccine arrived in 1955, the institute broadened to rehabilitation medicine in general. Her name continues in Allina Health's Courage Kenny Rehabilitation Institute, formed by a 2013 merger with Courage Center.
keyFacts: September 20, 1880: Born in Warialda, New South Wales. Some references give 1886, a year Kenny herself used.
1942: Guest instructor at the University of Minnesota Medical School.
December 17, 1942: Clinic opened in the Lymanhurst building, Minneapolis.

people.name: Paul Wellstone
people.field: Public service, mental health policy, education
body: In October 2008, six years after his death, Congress passed a law bearing Paul Wellstone's name. The Paul Wellstone and Pete Domenici Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act required insurers that cover both mental health and physical illness to cover them on equal terms. It capped a fight he had carried for years.

Wellstone came to Minnesota in 1969 as a young political science professor at Carleton College in Northfield. In 1990 he won an underdog race for the U.S. Senate against incumbent Rudy Boschwitz, campaigning from a beat-up green bus.

In the Senate he became an outspoken advocate for people with mental illness. In 1996 he and Republican Senator Pete Domenici of New Mexico won a first, limited parity law. After his death, his son David lobbied Congress for years to pass the broader one.

On October 25, 2002, eleven days before the election, Wellstone, his wife Sheila, their daughter Marcia, three campaign workers and two pilots died when their plane crashed near Eveleth on the Iron Range. A memorial stands south of Eveleth, reached by Bodas Road off Highway 53. Paul and Sheila Wellstone had worked together to end domestic violence. His political training work continued through Wellstone Action, renamed re:power in 2018.
keyFacts: October 25, 2002: Died in a plane crash near Eveleth.
October 2008: The broader parity act became law.

people.name: Toni Stone
body: In 1953 a woman took the field at second base for the Indianapolis Clowns of the Negro American League, filling the spot Hank Aaron had left when he moved to the major leagues. Her name was Toni Stone, and she had learned the game on the sandlots of St. Paul.

Marcenia Lyle Stone was born in Bluefield, West Virginia, and moved with her family to St. Paul when she was about ten. She grew up in the Rondo neighborhood, then the heart of the city's African American community, which was later split apart by construction of Interstate 94. By sixteen she was playing for the Twin City Colored Giants, a barnstorming team.

Before 1947 Black players were barred from Major League Baseball and formed their own leagues. As major league teams began signing Black stars, Negro League teams looked for new attractions. Stone became the first woman to play in the Negro American League.

It was not easy. Some teammates shunned her and told her to go home. She subtracted ten years from her age early on and kept it up throughout her career. When the Clowns' owner suggested she wear a skirt on the field, she refused and insisted on the regular uniform. She later played for the Kansas City Monarchs. She was honored by the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1991 and inducted into the Women's Sports Hall of Fame in 1993, and St. Paul named a neighborhood ballpark Toni Stone Field.
keyFacts: July 17, 1921: Born in Bluefield, West Virginia.
About 1931: Family moved to St. Paul; grew up in Rondo.
1937: Joined the Twin City Colored Giants.
1954: Played for the Kansas City Monarchs.
people.connectToWork: Does a form, category or rule in your work assume a person faces one barrier at a time? How would you find out what it misses?

people.name: Gordon Parks
body: In 1928 a teenager arrived in St. Paul from Fort Scott, Kansas, with almost nothing. His mother had just died, and he had come to live with an older sister, an arrangement that soon fell apart and left him homeless. Gordon Parks, the youngest of fifteen children, spent his difficult young years in the Twin Cities bussing tables, playing piano, and working as a railroad porter and waiter.

Parks attended Mechanic Arts and then Central High School in St. Paul but dropped out when the Great Depression cost him his job. He taught himself photography, and some of his earliest work was for the St. Paul Recorder and for Frank Murphy's Town and Country department store in St. Paul.

In April 1942 he received a Julius Rosenwald Fellowship, and that May he went to Washington, D.C., to work with the Farm Security Administration's photographers. In 1948, after a photo essay on a Harlem gang leader, Life magazine hired him as its first African American staff photographer. He stayed until 1972. He also wrote novels and memoirs, composed music and directed films, including The Learning Tree (1969), which made him the first African American to direct a major Hollywood film, and Shaft (1971).
keyFacts: November 30, 1912: Born in Fort Scott, Kansas.
1928: Moved to St. Paul after his mother's death.

people.name: Mee Moua
body: On January 29, 2002, voters on St. Paul's East Side went to the polls in a special election for an open state senate seat. Mee Moua won, and became the first Hmong American elected to a state legislature in the United States.

The Hmong are an ethnic group from the mountains of Laos and neighboring countries. After the Vietnam War era, thousands of Hmong people who had been caught up in the war spent years in refugee camps in Thailand before resettling in the United States, and St. Paul became home to one of the country's largest Hmong communities. Moua was born in Xieng Khouang, Laos. Her family spent several years in a refugee camp in Thailand and came to the United States when she was nine. She grew up in Appleton, Wisconsin.

She earned degrees from Brown University and the University of Texas and a law degree from the University of Minnesota in 1997, and led the Hmong Bar Association before running for office. She represented Senate District 67 from 2002 to 2010, was reelected twice and chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee.

After leaving the Senate she became a vice president at the Asian and Pacific Islander American Health Forum and, from 2012, president and executive director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice | AAJC in Washington, D.C. She left that post in March 2017 after five years.
keyFacts: June 30, 1969: Born in Xieng Khouang, Laos.
1997: J.D., University of Minnesota Law School.
January 29, 2002: Won a special election to the Minnesota Senate.
2002–2010: Served in the Senate; chaired the Judiciary Committee.

people.name: Prince
body: On August 3, 1983, Prince took the stage at First Avenue, a downtown Minneapolis nightclub, for a benefit concert for the Minnesota Dance Theatre. A mobile studio recorded the show, and those tapes became the basic tracks for "Purple Rain," "I Would Die 4 U" and "Baby I'm a Star." A year later the club was the backdrop for concert scenes in the film Purple Rain, and a kid from North Minneapolis became one of the biggest stars in the world.

Prince Rogers Nelson was born at Mount Sinai Hospital in Minneapolis, one of the first private hospitals in the Twin Cities to admit minority doctors, to John L. Nelson and Mattie Della Shaw, both local musicians.

He could have moved to Los Angeles or New York. Instead he spent most of his life in the Twin Cities. In 1987 he built Paisley Park, an estate and recording studio in the suburb of Chanhassen. The blend of funk, rock and R&B that he and his peers created became known as the Minneapolis Sound. He won seven Grammy Awards and an Academy Award for the music of Purple Rain, and entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2004.
He died at Paisley Park on April 21, 2016, at age 57. Paisley Park now operates as a museum and live music venue.
keyFacts: 2004: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

people.name: Earl Bakken
body: On October 31, 1957, a power blackout hit the Twin Cities. At the University of Minnesota, heart surgeon C. Walton Lillehei relied on pacemakers that depended on wall current to keep young patients' hearts beating after surgery. Many published accounts say one of his young patients died during the outage, though University of Minnesota archivists have questioned that story. Lillehei asked an engineer he had worked with, Earl Bakken, whether he could build something that did not depend on the power company.

Working from a magazine circuit for a transistorized metronome, Bakken built within about a month the first external, battery-powered, transistorized, wearable pacemaker, a small box that patients could carry with them.

Bakken was born in Columbia Heights, served as a radar instructor for the U.S. Army during World War II, and earned an electrical engineering degree from the University of Minnesota in 1948. In 1949 he and his brother-in-law, Palmer Hermundslie, founded Medtronic in Minneapolis to repair and maintain hospital equipment. The business struggled at first. It grew into one of the world's largest medical device companies.

Bakken moved to the island of Hawaii in 1994. There he chaired the board of the Five Mountain Medical Community as it developed North Hawaii Community Hospital, and he helped establish Tutu's House, a community health and education resource center, and the Kohala Center. He died in 2018 at age 94.
keyFacts: 1948: Electrical engineering degree, University of Minnesota.

people.name: Maria Sanford
body: In 1909, at age 72, Maria Sanford stood before graduates of the University of Minnesota to give the commencement address. MNopedia calls her the first woman to do so at a major university. For nearly thirty years she had taught rhetoric and oratory on the Minneapolis campus, and many had come to call her "the best-loved woman in Minnesota."

Sanford was born in Saybrook, Connecticut. At fifteen she asked her parents to let her use her dowry money to attend New Britain Normal School, a teacher-training school. She graduated with honors in 1855 and spent twelve years teaching in Connecticut. In 1867 she moved to Pennsylvania, where she narrowly lost a race for county superintendent of schools at a time when women could not vote.

In 1869 Swarthmore College hired her to teach history, which made her one of the first women professors in the nation, and in 1870 she became a full professor. In 1880 William Watts Folwell, president of the young University of Minnesota, recruited her. She lectured widely across the state, work that grew more important after a bad investment in the 1880s left her $30,000 in debt. She paid her way by speaking.

The University named its first women's dormitory, Sanford Hall, for her in 1910. In 1920 she was chosen to speak at the state's celebration of the Nineteenth Amendment. She died that April in Washington, D.C., during a speaking tour. In 1958 Minnesota placed her statue in the U.S. Capitol's Statuary Hall.
keyFacts: 1869: Hired by Swarthmore College; professor in 1870.
1880: Joined the University of Minnesota faculty.
1909: Retired and gave the commencement address.

people.name: Harry A. Blackmun
body: On June 9, 1970, Harry Blackmun took his oath as an associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court. He was the third nominee President Richard Nixon had sent to the Senate for the seat Abe Fortas had left, and he served for twenty-four years.

Blackmun was born in Nashville, Illinois, and grew up in St. Paul. He earned degrees from Harvard College in 1929 and Harvard Law School in 1932, then came back to Minnesota as law clerk to Judge John B. Sanborn of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, the federal appeals court whose territory includes Minnesota.

From 1934 to 1950 he practiced law in Minneapolis. In 1950 he became counsel to the Mayo organizations in Rochester, working for nearly a decade with Mayo Clinic doctors and administrators. In 1959 President Eisenhower appointed him to the Eighth Circuit seat his old mentor had held.

On the Supreme Court he wrote the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade (1973), which recognized a constitutional right to abortion and was overturned by the Court in 2022. His opinions drew both praise and sharp criticism. He took senior status in 1994 and died in Arlington, Virginia, in 1999.

people.name: Eugenie Anderson
body: On October 12, 1949, President Harry Truman announced that he would send a farm wife from Red Wing, Minnesota, to Copenhagen as U.S. ambassador to Denmark. Eugenie Anderson became the first woman in American history to hold the rank of ambassador.

She was born Helen Eugenie Moore in Adair, Iowa. She met John Pierce Anderson at Carleton College, married him in 1930, and settled on his family's farm, Tower View, in Red Wing. A 1937 trip to Germany, then under Nazi rule, turned her toward the study of international relations.

Minnesota's Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party was born from a 1944 merger. Anderson helped organize it with Hubert Humphrey and helped push Communist factions out of the new party in 1946–1947. By 1948 she was Minnesota's Democratic national committeewoman.

In Denmark she served from 1949 to 1953, and in 1951 she signed a U.S.–Danish treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation, the first woman to sign such a pact. Back home she chaired the Minnesota Commission for Fair Employment Practices from 1955 to 1960. President Kennedy sent her to Bulgaria in 1962, where she served until December 1964. She later represented the United States on the United Nations Trusteeship Council. She died in Red Wing on March 31, 1997.
keyFacts: 1944: Helped unify the Democratic and Farmer-Labor parties.
1955–1960: Chaired the Minnesota Commission for Fair Employment Practices.
1965–1968: U.S. representative on the UN Trusteeship Council.

people.name: Charles M. Schulz
body: On October 2, 1950, seven American newspapers printed a new comic strip about a round-headed boy named Charlie Brown. It was called Peanuts, and its creator was a young man who had spent years drawing in Minnesota.

Charles Schulz, a barber's son, was born in Minneapolis in 1922 and grew up in St. Paul. At thirteen he entered St. Paul Central High School as its youngest student, and he graduated in 1940. He learned to draw through a correspondence course from a Minneapolis school, the Federal Schools, later called Art Instruction Schools.

In February 1943 his mother died, and later that year he was drafted. He served as a squad leader in the 20th Armored Division in Europe in the last months of World War II. When he came home, Art Instruction hired him as a teacher.

His first weekly cartoon, Li'l Folks, began running in the St. Paul Pioneer Press in 1947. In 1950 United Feature Syndicate bought the strip and renamed it Peanuts, and Schulz drew every strip himself for nearly fifty years. He won the National Cartoonist Society's Reuben Award in 1955 and 1964, and A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965) won an Emmy and a Peabody. He died in Santa Rosa, California, on February 12, 2000. His last original Sunday strip ran the next day.
keyFacts: 1940: Graduated from St. Paul Central High School.
1943: Drafted; served with the 20th Armored Division.
1947: Li'l Folks began in the St. Paul Pioneer Press.
October 2, 1950: Peanuts debuted in seven newspapers.
February 12, 2000: Died in Santa Rosa, California.

people.name: Herb Brooks
body: In February 1980, at the Winter Olympics in Lake Placid, New York, a team of American college players beat the Soviet Union, the strongest hockey team in the world, 4–3. Two days later they beat Finland 4–2 to win the gold medal. The upset became known as the Miracle on Ice, and the coach who built that team was Herb Brooks of St. Paul.

As a senior at St. Paul's Johnson High School, Brooks won the state high school hockey championship. He turned down the University of Michigan to play for the University of Minnesota. In 1960 he was the last player cut from the U.S. Olympic team that went on to win gold at Squaw Valley.

He became head coach of the Minnesota Gophers in 1972 and led them to NCAA championships in 1974, 1976 and 1979. After 1980 he coached in the National Hockey League with the New York Rangers, Minnesota North Stars, New Jersey Devils and Pittsburgh Penguins, and in 2002 he coached the U.S. men to Olympic silver in Salt Lake City.
Brooks died on August 11, 2003, when his minivan veered off Interstate 35 near Forest Lake. He was inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 2006.
keyFacts: 1960: Last player cut from the U.S. Olympic team.
1974, 1976, 1979: NCAA titles as Gophers head coach.
February 1980: Olympic gold at Lake Placid.
August 11, 2003: Died on I-35 near Forest Lake.

people.name: Rick Cardenas
people.field: Disability rights, self-advocacy, Latino community organizing
body: In 1987 Rick Cardenas talked four St. Paul City Council members into using wheelchairs to travel around downtown, so they could experience what he and others dealt with every day. Access Press lists it among many campaigns, including access at Galtier Plaza, the World Trade Center, downtown skyways, the State Fair and the Capitol complex.

Richard Cardenas was born in St. Paul on February 9, 1942, one of four children of Manuel and Helen Cardenas. His family faced racial discrimination, and they were forced to move in the mid-1950s during freeway construction and urban renewal. He was a three-sport athlete at Harding High School. In 1960, at 18, on a trip before reporting for Army service, he was in a car accident that left him quadriplegic. He recalled that no state services existed then, and that his parents and brother acted as his attendants. His brother Manuel was later killed in Vietnam.

He taught high school dropouts at the Guadalupe Area Project on St. Paul's West Side, joined the United Farm Workers' boycotts, and helped found CLUES (Chicanos Latinos Unidos En Servicio) in 1981. He graduated from Hamline University, struggling to get into campus buildings along the way, and worked as a constituent outreach advocate for Senator Paul Wellstone.

For many years, until 2015, he was co-director of Advocating Change Together. Cliff Poetz of the University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration called him the chief organizer of Remembering With Dignity, which replaced numbered headstones at state institution cemeteries with people's names, and credited him with a key role in the Legislature's 2010 apology. In 2014 officials cut the ribbon on the Cardenas Connection, an elevator and stair tower linking the St. Paul skyway to the Green Line.

He died in March 2021, at 79. Minnesota law now names the Rick Cardenas Statewide Self-Advocacy Network, a state grant program for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, which must be governed by people with those disabilities.
keyFacts: 2014: Cardenas Connection tower opened in St. Paul.
March 2021: Died. Minn. Stat. 256.477 names the statewide self-advocacy network for him.

people.name: Margot Imdieke Cross
body: Margot Imdieke Cross used a wheelchair from age 2. She worked for more than 35 years at the Minnesota Council on Disability, where, by the council's account, she was the State of Minnesota's only accessibility specialist. She consulted on the Minnesota Senate Building, State Capitol Complex renovations, Target Field, U.S. Bank Stadium, CHS Field, Allianz Field and Target Center renovations.

She wrote expert opinions on state and federal access codes, championed accessibility in Minnesota state parks and trails, helped pass disability rights legislation, and consulted with thousands of architects, designers, contractors and builders. The council says that solving one person's access problem at a time brought her the most satisfaction.

She joined the first Wilderness Inquiry trip for people with disabilities in 1977 and later served on its board, and sat on the board of the Metropolitan Center for Independent Living. She attended the 1990 signing of the Americans with Disabilities Act, was the first recipient of the Access Press Charlie Smith Award, served as a Minneapolis Civil Rights Commissioner, and chaired the Minneapolis Advisory Committee on People with Disabilities.
The council announced her death on July 26, 2024. On June 26, 2025, it dedicated an accessible conference room in her name.
keyFacts: More than 35 years at the Minnesota Council on Disability.
1977: Joined the first Wilderness Inquiry trip for people with disabilities.
First recipient of the Access Press Charlie Smith Award.

institutions.name: Guthrie Theater
body: On September 30, 1959, three theater professionals, the British director Tyrone Guthrie, Oliver Rea and Peter Zeisler, placed an advertisement in the New York Times asking which American cities might want a professional resident theater. Seven cities responded, and Minneapolis drew Guthrie's strongest interest.

The T.B. Walker Foundation donated land next to the Walker Art Center, and Minnesotans raised more than $2.2 million. On May 7, 1963, the Guthrie opened with Hamlet, directed by Guthrie himself, with George Grizzard as Hamlet and Jessica Tandy as Gertrude. The first season began with 22,000 season ticket holders.

In 1963 most serious American theater was centered in New York. In 2006 the company moved to a new building by the French architect Jean Nouvel on the Mississippi riverfront. As of October 2026, Joseph Haj, who arrived in 2015, is artistic director.
keyFacts: September 30, 1959: Founders' New York Times advertisement.
2006: Moved to the Jean Nouvel building.

institutions.name: Minnesota State Fair
institutions.type: Annual state fair and agricultural exposition
institutions.location: Falcon Heights, between St. Paul and Minneapolis
body: Territorial fairs came first, in the mid-1850s. In 1859, a year after statehood, the first Minnesota State Fair was held in Minneapolis. The Minnesota State Agricultural Society, still the fair's governing body, was chartered in 1860.

For its first quarter century the fair moved between Minneapolis, St. Paul, Rochester, Red Wing, Owatonna and Winona. It was canceled in 1861 because of the Civil War and in 1862 after the U.S.–Dakota War. In 1885 Ramsey County donated land from its county poor farm, and the fair settled on its permanent grounds.

Theodore Roosevelt gave his "speak softly" speech there in 1901. John Philip Sousa debuted "The Minnesota March" in 1927, the year the Tilt-A-Whirl debuted. The first Princess Kay of the Milky Way was named in 1954, and butter sculptures of the winners began in 1965. The fair was also canceled in 1945 for wartime fuel shortages, in 1946 for a polio epidemic and in 2020 for COVID-19.

The fair's own figures count 1,923,325 visits over the twelve days of 2026, which counts visits, not different people. It publishes an accessibility guide and pages in Spanish, Hmong and Somali. The 2027 fair runs August 26 to September 6.
keyFacts: 1885: Permanent grounds on the former Ramsey County poor farm.
institutions.connectToWork: If you do outreach at a big public event, who would you reach, who would you miss, and what would you do for the people who are not there?

institutions.name: Walker Art Center
institutions.type: Contemporary art museum and sculpture garden
body: In 1879 Minneapolis lumberman T.B. Walker began inviting the public into his downtown home to see his art collection, which the museum says is often cited as the first public art gallery west of the Mississippi. After years of failed negotiations with the city over a museum, he built his own. The Walker Art Galleries opened on Lowry Hill on May 21, 1927. Walker died the next year, and his foundation kept the galleries open.

During the Depression, the Federal Art Project of the Works Progress Administration helped reopen the galleries, and on January 4, 1940, the institution became the Walker Art Center and turned toward modern art. A new building by Edward Larrabee Barnes opened in 1971. In 1988 the Walker and the Minneapolis park system opened the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden across the street, home to Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen's Spoonbridge and Cherry. A Herzog & de Meuron expansion opened in April 2005.
keyFacts: 1879: T.B. Walker opened his home gallery to the public.
May 21, 1927: Walker Art Galleries opened on Lowry Hill.
January 4, 1940: Became the Walker Art Center.
institutions.connectToWork: Which public service you rely on began as one person's private decision, and whose choices still shape who it serves?

institutions.name: The Arc Minnesota
body: In 1946 a group of parents and educators looking for options other than institutions founded the Minneapolis Association for Retarded Children, today's Arc Greater Twin Cities, by that group's own profile. The old name appears here only as history. In 1950 Minneapolis hosted the first national convention of the parents' organization that became The Arc. The Arc's national history says it was common then for doctors to tell parents that the best place for their child was an institution.
The state Arc office opened in May 1957, with Jerry Walsh as its first executive director, according to the Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities.

Today The Arc Minnesota says it works to promote and protect the human rights of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Its programs include individual advocacy, crisis housing assistance, housing services, a peer-to-peer mentor program, microgrants and self-advocacy. Arc's Value Village thrift stores help fund the work. Its toll-free help desk is 833-450-1494.
keyFacts: 1950: Minneapolis hosted the first national parents' convention.
institutions.connectToWork: What did past professional advice tell families about people like the one you are working with, and how might that history show up in your conversation today?

The Arc of the United States, Our History

institutions.name: Advocating Change Together
institutions.type: Self-advocacy organization led by people with disabilities
body: Advocating Change Together says it was founded by self-advocates in 1979, in response to growing concern that people with disabilities were being isolated and excluded from decisions about their own lives. The University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration, remembering co-founder Gloria Steinbring, calls it one of the first independent self-advocacy groups in the country.

Its current programs include community events, the Side by Side People's Chorus, an Olmstead Academy, a state self-advocacy conference, a Disability Pride Festival, Remembering With Dignity and support for Self-Advocates Minnesota.

Self-advocates formed Remembering With Dignity in 1994 with support from ACT and other Twin Cities groups. About 13,000 people who died in Minnesota's state hospitals had been buried under a number or with no marker. The group first won state funding in 1997 and held its first dedication in Faribault in 1999. According to MNopedia, about 8,000 gravestones had been installed as of 2020, with about 5,000 graves still waiting. The group helped draft the apology resolution signed in 2010.
keyFacts: About 8,000 named gravestones as of 2020, of about 13,000 graves.
institutions.connectToWork: Who sets the agenda when your team asks disabled people for input, and what decisions and money do they actually control?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Minnesota culture means the state's own systems, history and everyday habits that staff bring to their work, whatever their background. Minnesotans differ widely by region, generation, faith and ancestry. We found almost no research on how Minnesota's style of communication affects asking for help: one small student study, plus popular commentary. We say which is which below.
questions: What words do you use for your situation? Do you prefer "disabled person", "person with a disability", or other words?
Who gave you a label or diagnosis, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
What do you want? Who do you want helping you decide?
What isn't working? It helps me if you tell me plainly. Is there a way you would rather tell me?
Have you or your family ever had anything to do with a state hospital or institution? Would it help me to know about that?
Have you ever said "it's fine" to someone like me because it was easier? What would make it easier to say what's really going on?
Which people or groups do you already lean on, such as a congregation, a parent group or other self-advocates? Would you like any of them involved?
Would you like to meet other self-advocates or a peer mentor, or would you rather not?
How would you like to get information from me: in writing, in plain language, with an interpreter, or some other way?

context.heading: How state institutions shaped what families remember
body: Minnesota opened its hospital system in stages. Faribault began in 1879 as an experimental department of the Institute for the Deaf, Dumb, and Blind. Cambridge opened in 1925 as the Colony for Epileptics and closed in 1997. The Arc's national history says it was common for doctors to tell parents that an institution was the best place for their child.

Reform came in the 1940s and 1950s, driven by workers, faith groups, journalists and Governor Luther Youngdahl, who gave nine speeches on the topic between 1948 and 1950, according to the Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities. The same source says state schools stayed badly overcrowded into the 1950s, with Faribault more than 60 percent over capacity.

So when someone distrusts the state, that may come from this history as well as from recent experience. Ask rather than assume, and keep in mind that the reason may be something else entirely, such as a recent denial.

sources.label: MNHS library guide, Faribault State School & Hospital
MNHS library guide, Cambridge State Hospital
The Arc of the United States, Our History
Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities, "1940s to 50s: Lighting the Fire"

context.heading: Parents organizing, and people speaking for themselves
body: Minnesota's service system was shaped by organized parents and, later, by people with disabilities themselves. These are different voices, and they do not always agree. State law now funds a statewide self-advocacy network that must be governed by people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (Minn. Stat. 256.477).

Starting in 1994, self-advocates set out to restore the names of about 13,000 people buried under numbers or with no marker at state hospitals. In 2010 the Legislature passed an apology resolution, signed by Governor Pawlenty. MNopedia notes that supporters called it a landmark and that many saw it as overshadowed by budget cuts to disability and mental health services.

context.heading: The Jensen settlement and the Olmstead Plan
body: In 2009 the families of three residents of a state facility for adults with developmental disabilities filed a class action against the Department of Human Services over what they called inhumane use of restraints. It settled in 2011. The settlement required Minnesota to write an Olmstead Plan within 18 months, and a 2019 article in the Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law says it took about four years.
This page does not cover waiver history or the end of court oversight in the Jensen case. The Department of Human Services' own records are the place for those.

sources.label: Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law, 47(4):408 (2019)

context.heading: Politeness, indirect speech and what "fine" may mean
body: The phrase "Minnesota nice" comes mostly from popular writing. In a 2014 Star Tribune commentary, Jerilyn Veldof and Corey Bonnema described polite friendliness, understatement, reluctance to make a fuss and passive aggressiveness. These are observations by writers, not findings.

One study we found tested the idea: a 2016 University of Minnesota undergraduate thesis by Yezhenzi Kuang compared 129 people who named Minnesota as home, mostly introductory psychology students, with 377 others recruited online. The Minnesota group scored higher on trust and lower on verbal non-supportiveness, and the measures did not support the passive-aggressive description. The Minnesota group averaged about 21 years old and was about 87 percent white. It says nothing about any one person, and it did not study disability or asking for help.

Our own inference, not a finding: a person may say "doing fine" or turn down help for many reasons, and a worker may soften bad news so much that it is missed. Do not read silence or "it's fine" as agreement. Check back in writing and in plain language.

sources.label: Kuang, "The investigation of Minnesota Nice in terms of trust, communication style and personality," University of Minnesota (2016)

context.heading: Habits to check in your own work
body: If you soften a denial or a deadline, the person may not understand it. State the decision, the reason and the appeal rights clearly, in short sentences, and give a written summary. Define words like "waiver" and "assessment". These steps are practice suggestions drawn from this research, not tested methods.

Ask the person first, even if family speaks first. Offer self-advocacy and peer connections as options, never as requirements. Offer interpreters, including ASL, even when the person speaks English in conversation.

Old records and organization names use words such as "retarded", "feeble-minded" and "epileptic colony". Use them only when quoting history. Minnesota's statute says "persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities", and some disabled advocates prefer "disabled people". Some Deaf people use "Deaf" as a cultural identity. Ask each person what they prefer.

communityRoutes.name: Advocating Change Together
communityRoutes.purpose: Self-advocacy organization in St. Paul, led by people with disabilities, with training, a state conference and support for Self-Advocates Minnesota.

communityRoutes.name: NAMI Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: Free support groups, classes and a helpline for people with mental illness and their families. Phone 651-645-2948. For a crisis, call or text 988.

organizations.intro: Many of the bodies that carry Minnesota's shared public life are created in state law, such as the Minnesota Historical Society, founded in 1849, and the State Arts Board and 11 regional arts councils. Others are statewide disability organizations and independent newsrooms. The list is a starting point for learning. It is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

sources.label: Minnesota State Arts Board, Regional Arts Councils
Metropolitan Regional Arts Council, "What Is MRAC?"

entries.name: Minnesota Historical Society
entries.purpose: Founded in 1849. Collections, historic preservation and 26 historic sites and museums, including the Minnesota History Center and the Gale Family Library, plus MNHS Press.

entries.name: Minnesota Humanities Center
entries.purpose: Public humanities programs, grants, and an East Side event center. Founded in 1971 as the Minnesota Humanities Commission and renamed in 2007.

entries.name: Explore Minnesota
entries.purpose: The state's tourism office. Trip planning, tourism business support, and a part in the Outdoor Recreation Industry Partnership.

entries.name: Minnesota State Arts Board
entries.purpose: State arts grants and fiscal agent for legislative funding to the 11 regional arts councils. Traces to the State Art Society of 1903.

entries.name: Minnesota Regional Arts Councils
entries.purpose: Regional arts grants and support for artists and organizations. Every county is covered by one council. The system dates to 1977. The Metropolitan Regional Arts Council serves the seven metro counties and links to the other ten.
entries.linkLabel: Metropolitan Regional Arts Council's guide to the councils

entries.name: Minnesota Council on Disability
entries.location: St. Paul, 1600 University Avenue W, Suite 8
entries.purpose: Public policy, training and technical assistance, including disability parking, service animals, accessible housing and digital accessibility.

entries.name: Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities
entries.purpose: Federally mandated developmental disabilities council. It created Partners in Policymaking in 1987 and publishes a history of disability in Minnesota.

entries.name: Minnesota Disability Law Center
entries.location: Minneapolis, 111 N. Fifth Street, Suite 100; statewide
entries.purpose: Minnesota's federally designated Protection and Advocacy agency, part of Mid-Minnesota Legal Aid. Free disability rights legal help, facility monitoring and voter access work.

entries.name: MinnPost
entries.purpose: State and city politics, the congressional delegation, health, environment and arts, with reporting on Greater Minnesota.

entries.name: Minnesota Reformer
entries.purpose: State government, politics and policy. Launched January 14, 2020, as part of States Newsroom.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Reports for Minnesota's immigrants and communities of color. Founded in August 2019 by Mukhtar M. Ibrahim.

entries.name: Racket
entries.purpose: News, culture and food in an alt-weekly style. Launched in August 2021 by four former City Pages editors.

entries.name: Axios Twin Cities
entries.purpose: A local newsletter on Twin Cities news.

entries.name: Minnesota Monthly
entries.purpose: Travel, food, arts, culture, health and style.

entries.name: Mpls.St.Paul Magazine
entries.purpose: Twin Cities lifestyle, dining and culture.

entries.name: National Alliance on Mental Illness
entries.purpose: Education programs, support groups and a HelpLine at 800-950-6264, in English and Spanish. The HelpLine is peer support, not a crisis line. For a crisis, call or text 988. NAMI Minnesota is the state chapter.

entries.name: American Association of People with Disabilities
entries.purpose: A national, disability-led, cross-disability civil rights group working to increase the political and economic power of people with disabilities.

entries.name: The Arc of the United States
entries.purpose: Founded in 1950. Policy, legal advocacy and local chapters for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families. The Arc Minnesota is a chapter.

entries.name: National Council on Independent Living
entries.purpose: Founded in 1982. The membership body for Centers for Independent Living and Statewide Independent Living Councils.

entries.name: National Disability Rights Network
entries.purpose: The membership organization for the federally mandated Protection and Advocacy systems and Client Assistance Programs, including the Minnesota Disability Law Center.

entries.name: Easterseals
entries.purpose: A national network of affiliates offering disability and community services. Founded in 1919 in Elyria, Ohio. Use its finder to see what serves Minnesota.

entries.name: National Council on Disability
entries.purpose: Nine members advise the President, Congress and federal agencies on disability policy. In 1986 it recommended the ADA and later drafted the first version of the bill. Publishes yearly progress reports.

entries.name: Disability Scoop
entries.purpose: Developmental disability news on autism, intellectual disability, cerebral palsy and Down syndrome. Founded in 2008 by journalists Michelle Diament and Shaun Heasley.

entries.name: The Mighty
entries.purpose: First-person stories on disability, chronic illness, rare disease and mental health, mostly written by members. Founded in 2014 by Mike Porath.

entries.name: Rooted in Rights
entries.location: Washington State, a program of Disability Rights Washington
entries.purpose: Accessible digital media on disability, made by disabled storytellers, including a documentary project on deinstitutionalization.

entries.name: New Mobility
entries.location: National, published by United Spinal Association
entries.purpose: Life with spinal cord injury and related disabilities, for wheelchair users. Its print edition ended after the November/December 2024 issue, and it continues online.

entries.name: ABILITY Magazine
entries.purpose: Disability awareness, health, employment and inclusion. Founded in 1990.
